title: the ranges ahead
hook: a queen in a gambling hall asks a question the elders in the room cannot settle, and a poet in the hills answers in her own voice
carry: listen to it in her own words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bilva tree, and a hunter who kept Shiva's holy night without knowing it. Today, another ridge.
screen: `THE RANGES AHEAD.` · `A NIGHT KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: This year, in the dice game, Draupadi was dragged into a hall full of men and asked them a question. Had her husband lost himself before he staked her? If he had, was she his to lose? Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was too subtle for him to decide. Young Vikarna spoke up for her and was shouted down. The question hung in the air of the Mahabharata and never quite came down. Draupadi's voice reaches readers inside a vast story told about her. But some women in this tradition left their own words behind. A season of them waits in year four.
screen: `DRAUPADI'S QUESTION.` → `THE ELDERS CAN'T SETTLE IT.` → `WOMEN, IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The plan for that season is simple to say. The tradition's women, from the epics and from the saints: Sita, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Savitri, Damayanti, Shakuntala, and then Andal, Mirabai, Akka Mahadevi and Lal Ded. And wherever they left words of their own, those words, not only words about them. Two of those names, Akka and Lalla, haven't come up on this path yet, so here's a first look. Akka Mahadevi sang in Kannada, in short free poems called vachanas, sayings. Again and again her poems speak to one beloved, her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna, the lord white as jasmine. The story told about her says she left her home and walked out into the world to find him, covered only by her own long hair. Some readers hear her poems as blunt and tender at once: a woman telling God, plainly, that she will have no other. Far to the north, in Kashmir, Lal Ded, also called Lalla, left sayings in Kashmiri. In one saying attributed to her, in paraphrase, she tells how she wandered far, searching, and found what she was looking for at home, inside. Look at the range from here. In the epics, women like Draupadi, Kunti and Gandhari stand at some of the story's hardest turns and say the thing no one wants said. In the saints, women like Andal, Mira, Akka and Lalla speak about God in the first person, in their own languages. Year four sets those voices side by side. Not as a special topic. As part of the main road.
screen: `FROM THE EPICS AND THE SAINTS.` · `AKKA: THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE.` · `LALLA: SEARCHED FAR, FOUND AT HOME.` · `THE HARDEST TURNS, THE FIRST PERSON.` · then, large: `PART OF THE MAIN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman whose voice shaped yours: a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt, a friend. Not what people said about her, but something she herself said, a phrase you can still hear in her tone. Rest with it for a few breaths; if more of her words come, let them, and if only one, that's enough.
Vachana. A saying: Akka Mahadevi's short free poems to Shiva, one voice among the women of the tradition heard in their own words.
Your line: listen to it in her own words. Tomorrow, one more ridge. Day one thousand fifty-six.

howItsDone: Akka Mahadevi's vachanas are sung and recited in Karnataka, Lal Ded's sayings are quoted in Kashmir, and the women of the epics are honored in stories, songs and festivals across India.

fork.reveal: she asks the question of the whole assembly. Bhishma calls dharma too subtle to decide, and the elders give her no clear answer.

chat.says: Did any women in Hindu tradition leave their own words, not just stories about them?
options: Yes: Akka Mahadevi's Kannada vachanas, and Lal Ded's Kashmiri sayings.
No: women appear only as characters in stories men wrote down.
Only Draupadi, whose speeches in the epic she wrote herself.
chat.meaning: Akka Mahadevi sang vachanas in Kannada to Shiva; Lal Ded left sayings in Kashmiri. Year four reads their own words.

notes: Third of 'the ranges ahead' (1054–1059): year four's 'epics revisited: the women' block (weeks 39–44 in the outline), names taken from the outline. Days 1057–1059 (another writer) preview the Vedas, the schools of thought and the Upanishads, so this day takes the women rather than the darshanas.
Draupadi's question (Sabha Parva) was taught in year three (days 772–777); it's recalled briefly here.

Akka Mahadevi: Kannada vachanas, the signature Chennamallikarjuna glossed as 'the lord white as jasmine', and the hagiographic detail that she wandered covered only by her hair (framed as 'the story told about her'). Confirm.

Lal Ded: the 'searched far, found it at home' saying is a widely cited vakh but attribution and wording vary; it's framed as 'attributed to her'. Check against Grierson and Barnett (1920), public domain but not on the validator's list.
'Women like Draupadi, Kunti and Gandhari often stand at the story's hardest turns' is an interpretive line; confirm.
